before:
require "csv" loads the available CSV library. CSV.parse handles delimiters inside quoted fields; splitting each line on commas does not. With headers: true, the first row names columns instead of becoming a data record.

With headers: true, CSV.parse returns a CSV::Table containing header-addressable CSV::Row objects. table.first selects the first data row; ["topic"] reads that row's field by header name. The returned field is still text.

A CSV row supports header lookup, and values remain strings unless conversion is explicitly chosen. Missing or duplicate headers and field-size limits require a deliberate import policy; this fixed example assumes exactly the shown two headers.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
require "csv"
data = "topic,minutes\n\"read, reflect\",15\n"
table = CSV.parse(data, headers: true)
puts table.first["topic"]
puts table.first["minutes"]

```

Expected output or behavior: read, reflect
15. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
require "csv"
data = "topic,minutes\n\"read, reflect\",15\n"
table = CSV.parse(data, headers: true)
puts table.first["topic"]
puts table.first["minutes"]
```
The output is `read, reflect`, then `15`. Read, reflect is one topic. The minutes field is still fifteen.
